title: Keeping property, people, money, and maintenance connected
audience: A curious adult from another field. No knowledge of property management, accounting, tenancy law, or business software is assumed.
scope: An introduction to the ongoing management of property and the software supporting it. The recurring example is a Dutch apartment building with rental homes and an owners' association. Commercial leases and other countries, including Germany, have different rules. Buying an investment, mortgage advice, and detailed legal procedures are outside this guide. Canal Court, its people, contracts, prices, and financial examples are fictional.
learningGoals: Explain how property management connects a physical place, its users, agreements, money, and upkeep.
Distinguish ownership from tenancy and management, and an apartment from shared building parts.
Follow rent administration and a repair through the people and records involved.
Explain why a payment, an invoice, a completed job, and a useful report are different things.

introduction.whatItIs: Imagine renting a flat. You receive keys, pay agreed charges, and contact someone when the roof leaks. Behind those ordinary moments, someone must know which home you rent, who owns it, what the agreement says, where payments belong, and who can authorize repairs. Property management keeps these arrangements working over time.
introduction.whyItMatters: A property business may manage many buildings for different owners. A wrong link can send a bill to the wrong person or leave a repair waiting with the wrong team. Real estate ERP software connects the records and workflows. ERP means enterprise resource planning: here, shared administration for properties, contracts, finances, maintenance, and the people using them.
introduction.familiarComparison: Think of running a community center with several rooms, regular users, shared heating, and visiting repair companies. A room booking calendar is useful, but it cannot answer every question about agreements, bills, or the leaking roof.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: Property arrangements may last years, ownership can change, and tenants have rights that go beyond a booking. A manager can administer property without owning it. The software company provides tools; it does not become the landlord or perform the repair.

participants.name: The tenant or occupier
participants.role: Uses the premises under an agreement and communicates about payments, access, and problems. Sam rents apartment 2 at fictional Canal Court.
participants.caresAbout: A usable home, understandable charges, fair treatment, privacy, and clear responses when something goes wrong.

participants.name: The owner or investor
participants.role: Owns the property interest and makes decisions within the applicable rules. Ari owns and lets apartment 2.
participants.caresAbout: Reliable income, the condition of the property, costs, and responsibilities. An asset manager may help an investor make decisions across several properties.

participants.name: The property manager
participants.role: Handles agreed administration and coordination for an owner. Mira manages Ari's rental; her authority comes from the management arrangement.
participants.caresAbout: Clear responsibilities, accurate records, prompt service, and fees that cover the work. She needs to know which decisions she can make and which require approval.

participants.name: The owners' association
participants.role: Coordinates shared interests in an apartment building. In the Netherlands it is called a vereniging van eigenaars, or VvE. Apartment owners are its members.
participants.caresAbout: Shared maintenance, contributions, reserves, and properly recorded decisions. It is distinct from an individual landlord and from a firm hired to administer it.

participants.name: Contractors and other suppliers
participants.role: Inspect, repair, clean, or maintain property under an agreed scope. They need access and someone authorized to instruct the work.
participants.caresAbout: A clear problem description, safe access, timely decisions, and payment for work that has been properly agreed and checked.

participants.name: The software provider
participants.role: Supplies the system and services such as setup, migration, training, and support. Owners or management organizations pay for its use.
participants.caresAbout: Dependable records and workflows that customers can use effectively. Property rent and the provider's software fees are different revenue streams.

participantsOverview.illustrationPrompt: An extremely clear relationship map. One large card on the LEFT labeled 'Property manager' shows a woman at a desk. On the RIGHT, five small cards in a vertical column from top to bottom, labeled 'Tenant', 'Owner', 'Owners association', 'Contractor', 'Software provider'. Their simple icons respectively show a home user, person with property document, owners around a roof drawing, repair worker, laptop. Exactly FIVE separate plain lines fan from the manager card's right edge to the five right-hand cards, ONE line per card. No arrowheads, no second line to any card, no connecting the right-hand cards to each other. Above each line one label, respectively: 'Requests and updates', 'Mandate and reports', 'Shared-building coordination', 'Work coordination', 'Tools and support'. Keep lines and labels from crossing. No other words, numbers, charts, money, approval marks or decorative connectors. Large type and generous white space, navy teal amber on warm white. This is a coordination map, not an ownership or spending-authority chart.

media.title: Who connects property, agreements, and services
media.alt: The property manager coordinates tenant requests, the owner mandate and reports, shared-building matters with the owners association, contractor work, and tools and support with the software provider.
media.caption: The lines show coordination. Ownership, contractual authority, and permission to commit money still depend on the relevant arrangements.

concepts.meaning: A portfolio is a collection of properties managed or considered together. A building is a physical structure. A unit is a separately identified space, such as an apartment, shop, or parking place. Shared parts, such as a roof or stairwell, may need their own records and responsibilities.
concepts.example: Canal Court contains four apartments. Sam lives in unit 2, but the roof serves the building. Ari's ownership, Sam's tenancy, and Mira's management role must be linked to the right place and period.
concepts.whyItMatters: An address alone may be too broad to identify a contract or cost. The place where a problem appears is not always the part that needs repairing.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: A simple hierarchy of places, not an ownership diagram. Top small collection of three buildings labeled 'Portfolio'. A line highlights one building below labeled 'Building'. Show that building as a clean cutaway with FOUR apartments, only one highlighted and labeled 'Unit 2'. The shared roof is a single continuous roof across the building, labeled 'Shared roof'. Exactly these four text labels, no other unit numbers, money, owners, contracts or arrows implying ownership. Adult editorial navy teal amber, generous spacing.

media.title: Portfolio, building, and unit
media.alt: A portfolio contains several buildings. One building is shown with four apartments, unit 2 highlighted, and a single shared roof.
media.caption: The hierarchy identifies places. Ownership, tenancy, management, and responsibility for shared parts need their own linked records.

concepts.term: The lease and its effective dates
concepts.meaning: A lease, or tenancy agreement, records the right to use premises and the associated obligations. Important facts include the parties, unit, start date, charges, and permitted changes. Indexation means adjusting an amount using an agreed index, but a clause or software calculation still has to comply with applicable law.
concepts.example: Sam signs before moving in. The agreement's signing date, start date, payment dates, and any review date describe different events. A proposed rent change must use the correct clause, rules, and effective date.
concepts.whyItMatters: A date in the system can trigger invoices or notices. Copying the wrong date can affect someone's money or rights, so changes need review and a history.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: A horizontal timeline with three clearly separate stations. First labeled 'Signed' shows a pen and agreement. Second labeled 'Starts' shows a tenant arriving at an apartment. Third labeled 'Review' shows a person checking a document beside a calendar. A thin arrow indicates time progressing from left to right. No actual dates, no price increases, percentages, automatic renewal, automatic ending or eviction imagery. Bottom label 'Different dates, different effects'. All documents contain abstract lines only. Exactly four text labels.

media.title: The lease and its effective dates
media.alt: A timeline separates signing an agreement, starting a tenancy, and reviewing the agreement later.
media.caption: Signing, starting, and reviewing describe different events. Any change must follow the agreement and applicable rules.

concepts.term: Rent, service charges, and a security deposit
concepts.meaning: Rent pays for use of the premises. Service charges cover specified services or costs where the agreement and rules allow them, often through advances followed by a settlement. A security deposit is held as security and dealt with under the applicable conditions; it is not ordinary rent income.
concepts.example: Sam's illustrative monthly charge is €900 rent plus a €100 service-cost advance. A security deposit is recorded separately. If a year's advances total €1,200 and the permitted costs properly allocated to Sam are €1,080, the €120 difference is a credit to settle.
concepts.whyItMatters: Money can have different purposes even when the same organization administers it. An owner's full association contribution cannot simply be copied into the tenant's service charges.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three separate equally sized labeled containers, with no connecting arrows and no shared profit total. Container 1 'Rent' shows apartment keys. Container 2 'Service advances' shows a communal light and cleaning equipment beside a review document. Container 3 'Security deposit' shows a secure folder with a return-arrow icon. Bottom label 'Different purposes, separate records'. NO currency amounts, percentages, refunds promised unconditionally, money-growing plants, or words such as profit or revenue. Exactly four labels. Clear adult diagram on warm white.

media.title: Rent, service charges, and a security deposit
media.alt: Three separate cards show rent with keys, service advances with lighting, cleaning and a review document, and a security deposit with a secure folder and return symbol.
media.caption: Keep each payment purpose clear. Service advances need the applicable settlement, and a deposit is dealt with under its return and deduction conditions.

concepts.meaning: An invoice or rent charge records an amount due. A payment receipt records money received. Reconciliation matches the two and investigates differences. It includes checking the payer, reference, period, credits, and the correct owner or organization.
concepts.example: Mira records Sam's €1,000 monthly charge, but the bank shows €950 received. The €50 difference needs investigation. A payment might be incomplete, recorded against the wrong period, or not yet matched.
concepts.whyItMatters: Creating a charge does not collect the money. Automated reminders can be wrong if the payment records are incomplete or the charge is disputed.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Two large financial record cards on a desk. Left title 'Charge' with exactly '€1,000'. Right title 'Receipt' with exactly '€950'. A reviewer compares the cards with a magnifying glass. Between and below them an amber label 'Check the €50 difference'. No overdue stamp, fine, eviction symbol, automatic reminder, debt assumption or additional amounts. No equals sign. Exactly the two titles, two amounts and the question label. White space and large readable type.

media.title: Invoices, receipts, and reconciliation
media.alt: A reviewer compares a charge of €1,000 with a receipt of €950. An amber note says to check the €50 difference.
media.caption: A mismatch calls for investigation. Check the records and circumstances before deciding why the figures differ.

concepts.term: A repair request, a work order, and completion
concepts.meaning: A request describes a problem. A work order instructs an agreed task, with a location, responsible party, and scope. Completion means checking the agreed result and recording any remaining work. The request, repair, supplier bill, and payment are linked but separate records.
concepts.example: Sam reports water on the ceiling. An inspection identifies a roof problem. Sending a contractor does not prove that the leak and any agreed follow-up work have been resolved.
concepts.whyItMatters: Closing a ticket too early makes the dashboard look better while the person in the home still has a problem.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: A very simple four-scene teaching diagram. The ONLY words anywhere in the image are four large headings: 'Report', 'Authorize', 'Repair', 'Verify'. Beneath Report: a tenant points to a ceiling drip. Beneath Authorize: one person checks one sheet bearing ONLY a large roof icon and three abstract horizontal lines. Beneath Repair: a worker holds a tool beside a small roof model on a table. Beneath Verify: the same tenant and an inspector look at a dry ceiling. Three simple arrows connect the scenes from left to right. Leave generous white space. Absolutely no extra documents, text on documents, tiny letters, signatures, subheadings, captions, serial numbers, invoices, money or text decorations. Use clean flat navy teal amber adult illustration. These four scenes alone teach the distinction; surrounding prose supplies details.

media.title: A repair request, a work order, and completion
media.alt: Four scenes show reporting a ceiling leak, authorizing work, repairing a roof model, and checking the dry ceiling with the tenant.
media.caption: Follow the work through to a checked result, with any remaining work recorded. A supplier bill is a separate record.

concepts.meaning: Planned maintenance looks ahead to work such as roof renewal, painting, or equipment replacement. A reserve is money set aside for future needs. Dutch owners' associations have reserve requirements; a multi-year maintenance plan connects anticipated work, timing, and cost.
concepts.example: Canal Court's owners may need both a repair now and a larger roof project later. The association's plan and funds belong to its shared responsibilities, separate from Ari's rental accounts and Sam's security deposit.
concepts.whyItMatters: A quiet month without repair tickets does not mean the building needs no future spending. A forecast also does not prove the required money is already available.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three equally sized separate cards: 'Inspect' with a person inspecting a roof diagram; 'Plan' with a calendar showing three unnumbered future blocks and roof/painting icons; 'Fund' with a clearly labeled reserve folder and simple coin icon. Under the cards place the question 'Does the plan match the funds?'. No numerical forecast, percentage, equal sign, investment growth, tenant deposit, or guarantee that savings cover all future work. Four text labels only. The cards are related questions, not an automatic finance pipeline.

media.title: Planned maintenance and reserves
media.alt: Inspection, a calendar of future roof and painting work, and a reserve folder appear as three separate cards, followed by the question: Does the plan match the funds?
media.caption: Connect the building condition, planned work, and available funds. A forecast does not establish that the necessary money is already available.

concepts.term: Reports with a clear scope and period
concepts.meaning: A report needs to say whose properties it covers, for which period, and what it measures. Occupancy describes how much space is let on a stated basis. Rent charged, cash received, costs, and property value answer other questions. Owners and managers need these distinctions to interpret results.
concepts.example: Even if all four Canal Court apartments are let, that does not establish that all payments arrived. Ari's rental report should also be distinguishable from the owners' association's accounts.
concepts.whyItMatters: Combining figures from different owners, dates, or purposes can create a convincing but misleading total. A property valuation is an estimate of value, not cash in the bank.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: An extremely spare diagram with exactly THREE cards in one horizontal row, each containing one large heading and one simple icon, nothing else. Left heading 'Space let', icon of apartment doors with two occupied and one empty. Middle heading 'Amounts charged', icon of a single paper with three abstract lines. Right heading 'Cash received', icon of a bank and one coin. Beneath the row, plain text 'Which owner? Which period?'. These FOUR headings are the ONLY text in the image. Absolutely no explanatory sentences, subheadings, captions inside cards, additional lower cards, checkmarks, stamps, document text, bank labels, numbers, comparisons, arrows or extra teaching material. Most of the image is warm white space. Large navy text, simple navy teal amber icons. The three cards are separate views, not a process. The tutorial prose supplies every further explanation.

media.title: Reports with a clear scope and period
media.alt: Three report cards show space let, amounts charged, and cash received, with a shared question about the owner and reporting period.
media.caption: These views answer different questions. Define the properties, parties, and dates before interpreting or comparing totals.

historyNote: These selected Dutch milestones connect housing conditions, administrative tools, and tenant protections. They are not a complete history of property management. Other countries and commercial property have different histories and legal frameworks.

history.change: The Dutch Housing Act of 1901 responded to poor housing conditions and expanded the public role in housing standards and improvement.
history.whyItMatters: Property administration concerns the quality of places people use as well as the collection of payments.

history.change: As one Dutch example, Informant began developing standard property-management software in 1995 and brought it to market in 1998, according to its company history.
history.whyItMatters: Repeated tasks such as recording contracts and producing financial information became a focus for software designed around this particular trade.

history.change: The Dutch Good Landlordship Act took effect on 1 July 2023, addressing matters including written agreements, information for tenants, service costs, and undesirable landlord conduct.
history.whyItMatters: Clear records and communication help people understand and check how they are treated. Software must support the applicable requirements rather than assume an old template remains sufficient.

walkthrough.title: Mira manages Sam's tenancy and a roof leak
walkthrough.setup: Canal Court has four separately owned apartments and shared building parts. Ari lets apartment 2 to Sam; Mira manages that rental. Assume the building documents assign the roof work in this example to the owners' association. The association has its own decision process and accounts. All amounts and arrangements below are illustrative.

steps.title: Identify the place, parties, and authority
steps.whatHappens: Mira links apartment 2 to the building, Ari's ownership, and her management arrangement. She records the relevant association contacts and who can authorize different kinds of work.
steps.whyItMatters: Owning, living in, and managing the same place are different roles. Being able to edit a record does not itself authorize spending.

steps.title: Record the tenancy and hand over the home
steps.whatHappens: After the relevant checks, the parties agree the tenancy. Mira records its dates, the illustrative €900 rent and €100 service advance, and the deposit separately. The handover records the property's condition, keys, and contact arrangements.
steps.whyItMatters: The recurring administration should reflect the actual agreement, with useful evidence of the starting condition.

steps.title: Charge correctly and match the money
steps.whatHappens: The system produces the €1,000 monthly charge. A €950 bank receipt leaves €50 to investigate. In this case Sam identifies a transfer mistake and sends the remaining €50; Mira matches both receipts to the correct charge.
steps.whyItMatters: The resolution comes from checking the records and communicating, rather than treating a mismatch as automatic proof of misconduct.

steps.title: Investigate the reported leak
steps.whatHappens: Sam reports ceiling water. Mira assesses urgency through the agreed process, coordinates an inspection, and keeps Sam informed. The contractor identifies a shared-roof problem, so she involves the association's authorized representative.
steps.whyItMatters: The report belongs with Sam's home, while the repair also belongs with a shared building part and its decision-makers.
steps.watchOut: An urgent problem needs the applicable emergency response, while responsibility and cost allocation are recorded. The system should preserve both the resident's report and the linked shared-building work.

steps.title: Authorize, carry out, and verify the work
steps.whatHappens: The association arranges the shared work under its procedures. Mira coordinates access and updates Sam. After repair, the agreed result and any remaining damage are checked. The appropriate reviewer checks the supplier bill against the approved work.
steps.whyItMatters: An instruction, a contractor's completion message, an accepted result, and a paid bill are separate milestones.

steps.title: Close the records and plan ahead
steps.whatHappens: Mira records the outcome for Sam and Ari, while the association updates its own costs and maintenance plan. In the later annual service-cost review, €1,200 of Sam's advances is compared with €1,080 of permitted, properly allocated costs, producing a €120 credit to settle.
steps.whyItMatters: Ari's rental finances, the association's roof spending, and Sam's service-cost statement remain distinguishable. The roof expense is not automatically passed on to Sam.

walkthrough.outcome: Sam has a repaired home and understandable records. Ari can see the rental's financial position, and the association can account for shared work and future needs. Mira can trace the request, decisions, work, and bills without confusing one party's money or responsibilities with another's.
walkthrough.illustrationPrompt: Create a minimalist SIX-ICON workflow overview in a strict 3-column by 2-row grid on warm white. This is an icon diagram, with no people or realistic scenes. Each of the six cells contains ONE large simple flat icon group and ONE heading. The ONLY text in the entire image is these headings: '1 Identify', '2 Agree and hand over', '3 Match payments', '4 Investigate', '5 Repair and verify', '6 Report and plan'. Cell 1 icon: apartment building with three small role silhouettes. Cell 2 icon: handshake and key, no contract paper. Cell 3 icon: bank-building symbol with a magnifying glass, absolutely no papers, receipts, money amounts, bank balances, coins, screens or numbers. Cell 4 icon: ceiling-drop symbol and telephone handset. Cell 5 icon: roof with wrench and a separate verification check symbol. Cell 6 icon: two separate folders marked only by a building icon and a door icon, next to a blank calendar grid. NO other text, names, numbers beyond heading numbers, prices, monetary symbols, charts, tiny writing, documents, additional labels or arrows between cells. Never copy monetary amounts from the surrounding story into this diagram. The icons give orientation while all factual and financial details stay in the tutorial prose. Large readable navy headings, clear navy outlines, restrained teal and amber, very generous white space.

media.title: Mira follows the tenancy from setup through repair and reporting
media.alt: Six icon panels represent identifying the property and roles, agreeing and handing over, matching payments, investigating a leak, repairing and verifying, and reporting and planning.
media.caption: The tenant report, shared-roof repair, owner records, and future maintenance remain connected while their responsibilities and finances stay clear.

valueAndIncentives.title: The property must work for its users
valueAndIncentives.explanation: People need usable premises and dependable service. Owners need income and property that remains in good condition. Timely maintenance and clear communication can serve both interests.
valueAndIncentives.example: Resolving Sam's leak improves the home and helps prevent further building damage.

valueAndIncentives.title: Money belongs to different activities and parties
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Owners receive rent and bear relevant costs. Managers earn agreed management fees; contractors earn fees for services; software providers earn subscriptions and service fees. Associations collect contributions for shared purposes.
valueAndIncentives.example: Sam's €1,000 monthly charge is not €1,000 of revenue for Mira's management business or for its software provider.

valueAndIncentives.title: Efficiency needs a useful definition
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Less repeated data entry can reduce handling effort. But work is only improved if payments are correct, important dates are handled, and people get appropriate responses.
valueAndIncentives.example: Automatically closing repair tickets might reduce an apparent backlog without fixing any more roofs.

challenges.title: Maintaining a reliable history
challenges.whyHard: Owners, occupants, contracts, and charges change while the building stays at the same address. Old documents may still matter.
challenges.tradeOff: A simple current view is convenient, but past periods need their own accurate context.
challenges.example: Replacing Ari's name after a sale must not make last year's bills appear to belong to the new owner.
challenges.commonApproach: Keep dated relationships and review changes and imported records. A shared database can spread an incorrect link as efficiently as a correct one.

challenges.title: Knowing who decides and who pays
challenges.whyHard: A problem can affect a private unit and a shared building part. Ownership, tenancy, management authority, and insurance may point to different processes.
challenges.tradeOff: Prompt action matters, while commitments and charges must go to the correct parties.
challenges.example: Sam reports the leak, but the association authorizes the shared-roof work under the assumptions of this case.
challenges.commonApproach: Record responsibilities, approval limits, and escalation routes before problems arise. Handle urgency through the agreed process and investigate disputed allocation without losing the original request.

challenges.title: Applying local and contract-specific rules
challenges.whyHard: Residential and commercial property, countries, contract dates, and property categories can have different rules.
challenges.tradeOff: Automation saves effort on repeated work, but applying one rule everywhere can produce repeated mistakes.
challenges.example: A rent-review date does not mean the system may apply any chosen percentage.
challenges.commonApproach: Keep reviewed rules and source dates with the relevant contract types. Have qualified reviewers check consequential changes; a technically valid calculation can still use the wrong rule.

challenges.title: Balancing today's bills and tomorrow's building
challenges.whyHard: Large maintenance needs develop over years, while owners and associations manage nearer-term budgets.
challenges.tradeOff: Smaller contributions today may leave less money for future work; setting aside more has an immediate cost.
challenges.example: A patch can stop the current leak without eliminating the need for later roof renewal.
challenges.commonApproach: Connect inspections, a realistic maintenance plan, and available funds. Revisit estimates as the building changes; a plan is neither a guarantee of condition nor proof of funding.

challenges.title: Making financial explanations understandable
challenges.whyHard: Rent, deposits, service advances, owner contributions, and supplier costs can pass through related workflows while retaining different meanings.
challenges.tradeOff: Detailed records support accuracy, but unexplained categories can overwhelm tenants and owners.
challenges.example: Sam needs to understand the €120 service-cost credit without reading the association's entire accounts.
challenges.commonApproach: Use clear statements with traceable calculations and role-appropriate access. Keep human help available for questions; a portal or AI-written explanation cannot correct a misclassified cost by itself.

misconceptions.belief: The manager owns the property and can decide everything.
misconceptions.reality: Management authority comes from an arrangement and the applicable rules. The owner, association, or another party may need to decide.

misconceptions.belief: Every amount received is rent income.
misconceptions.reality: Deposits, advances, and money administered for others have different purposes. Record their meaning and the party they belong to.

misconceptions.belief: A fully let building means all the money has arrived.
misconceptions.reality: Occupancy and payment collection measure different things. Both need a clear reporting period and scope.

misconceptions.belief: A contractor's bill proves the repair is complete.
misconceptions.reality: The bill must be checked against the work and agreed result. A resident's unresolved problem should remain visible.

takeaways: Connect each place to the right people, agreement, period, and responsibility.
Keep rent, service costs, deposits, and association funds understandable and distinguishable.
Follow a repair from report to verified result, alongside its approvals and bills.
Good software supports dependable service and traceable decisions over the life of the property.

knowledgeChecks.question: Sam reports ceiling water in apartment 2, but inspection identifies a shared-roof problem. Should the record simply be moved away from Sam's home?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Keep Sam's report and link it to the shared-building work and the correct decision-makers.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The affected location, cause, and responsibility are related facts. Losing the original report would make follow-up with Sam harder.

knowledgeChecks.question: The system records a €1,000 charge and a €950 receipt. What should Mira do before treating the €50 difference as an overdue payment?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Check the period, reference, other receipts, credits, due date, and any dispute, and communicate as needed.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The difference needs reconciliation. A partial match alone does not establish why it exists.

knowledgeChecks.question: Sam paid €1,200 in service advances and the permitted costs properly allocated to Sam are €1,080. What does the difference represent?
knowledgeChecks.answer: A €120 credit to be settled through the applicable process, not additional rent income.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The advance and the supported final cost are different figures. The statement should make their relationship clear.

knowledgeChecks.question: The roof contractor sends a completion message, but agreed follow-up work remains. Is the entire case complete?
knowledgeChecks.answer: No. Record what was completed and keep the remaining work and communication visible.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: A contractor update, an accepted result, and financial settlement are separate milestones.

How do maintenance plans relate to available funds and current building condition?
